title: Lesson 40: Capstone: build your org's AI adoption plan
description: Grounded in Lesson 40 of the AI Adoption series: the six sections of an adoption plan and their page budget, why the baseline comes before the policy, the target size for a prohibited list, what the scope section must exclude, and the first ninety days of work after the plan is published.

questions.question: The capstone insists on a build order for the plan. What defect does it name for a plan written policy first and baseline last?
options: It produces a policy that is too long to be read in one sitting
It produces decision thresholds stated in risk terms instead of in money
A plan written as policy first and baseline last produces controls aimed at nothing
It produces a portfolio with no refusals recorded against revisit dates
questions.explanation: The lesson says a plan written as policy first and baseline last produces controls aimed at nothing, which it calls the most common defect in AI governance documents. That is why week one of the four-week build is the baseline, including the inventory reconciliation and the page listing what you cannot currently answer. Week three writes the controls, after scope, outcomes, and decision rights exist.

questions.question: Section three of the plan covers policy and controls. What target does the capstone set for the prohibited list?
options: Twenty items, each with a named owner and a review frequency
Four items on the prohibited list is a good target, because a prohibited list of twenty is a list nobody remembers.
No prohibited items, because a prohibition list removes the program's flexibility
Ten items, reviewed annually by the approving group
questions.explanation: The week three build step states that four items on the prohibited list is a good target, on the reasoning that a prohibited list of twenty is a list nobody remembers. The worked example follows the same rule: Marcus's policy lists four prohibitions alongside a three-tier data rule. The lesson's failure modes add that the plan's credibility comes from being short enough to quote from memory.

questions.question: In Marcus's one-page plan, what does the scope section explicitly exclude from year one?
options: Anything in the order-to-cash, resourcing, and bid production workflows
Anything above 25,000 dollars, which requires the approving group
Anything running on the assistant platform without a signed data processing agreement
Year one explicitly excludes anything that produces client-facing advice without a named human reviewer, and anything that makes a decision about a person.
questions.explanation: The scope section in the worked example states the three workflows year one covers and then states two exclusions: anything that produces client-facing advice without a named human reviewer, and anything that makes a decision about a person. The lesson argues the exclusions do more work than the inclusions, because they are what lets a team say no without escalating. The spend threshold and the data processing agreement come from the operating model and the policy sections, not the scope section.
